title: Temperature, Relative Humidity, VPD & Dew-Point Interpretation

content.overview: Temperature and relative humidity must be interpreted together because saturation vapor pressure changes with temperature. VPD is useful for describing atmospheric drying demand, while dew point helps evaluate condensation risk; neither is a stand-alone diagnosis of plant water status.

vocabulary.definition: The difference between saturation vapor pressure and actual vapor pressure for the defined temperature-moisture state.
The temperature at which air of a given moisture content becomes saturated and condensation can begin on a surface at or below that temperature.
The difference between measured leaf temperature and surrounding air temperature, which can change leaf-level vapor-pressure interpretation.

sections.title: RH alone is incomplete
sections.body: The same RH at two different temperatures represents different vapor-pressure conditions. Calculate or interpret VPD from the actual temperature/RH pair rather than treating RH as a fixed moisture-demand measure.

sections.title: Leaf temperature can differ from air
sections.body: Radiation, airflow and transpiration can make leaves warmer or cooler than nearby air. Leaf-level vapor-pressure interpretation therefore improves when representative leaf temperature is known.

sections.title: Dew point is a surface-risk concept
sections.body: Condensation becomes plausible when a leaf, wall, duct or other surface approaches or falls below dew-point temperature, even when bulk-room RH is below 100%.

workedExamples: Two rooms at 60% RH are not environmentally equivalent if one is substantially warmer; the warmer room generally has a different VPD because saturation vapor pressure is higher.
commonMistakes: Using one VPD value as a universal optimum for every cultivar/stage.
Assuming air temperature equals leaf temperature.
Treating VPD as a direct measurement of root-zone water status.
content.practicalApplication: For three supplied temperature/RH states, compare RH, VPD and dew-point implications, then explain how a cooler leaf or surface could change the plant-level or condensation interpretation.
content.summary: VPD and dew point are contextual environmental tools. Their usefulness depends on correct temperature, humidity, surface/leaf context and measurement quality.
